e1-emuA:
Most communes of my acquaintance failed from the inside, in one of two ways:

They may have had a brilliant solution for how to distribute property or labor, but when the deep waters of jealousy or childhood hurt or humiliation or attraction or resentment or grief came up, the group was without a common, well-honed method for dealing with it. They just became agenda items.
e1-emuB:
There seem to be two main internal reasons for communes to fail.

It’s because they don’t realize that it’s as important to equitably distribute the psychological messiness that goes along with people (jealousy, wounds from childhood, humiliation, sexual attraction, resentment, grief, etc) as it is to equitably distribute the ownership of the land and the amount of work. In the absence of this awareness these things don’t go away–they simply put themselves on the agenda.
e2-emuA:
The Federation of Egalitarian Communities and other income-sharing communities have developed some sophisticated systems for dealing with issues of labor, money, and decision-making. But the best meeting procedure in the world won’t make two people who hate each other like one another. At best, it will determine who gets to talk about their hatred, and whether they need a second.

Sooner or later, politics will deal with emotional material. People will argue about schedules, or committees, or noise, or food, or whatever – but not about the real issue at hand.
e2-emuB:
Meeting procedure isn’t going to solve every problem, no matter how sophisticated the system of labor and money and decision making may be in a community of the Federation of Egalitarian Communities or other income-sharing community. It can’t make it so that two people don’t hate each other. It can only make it so that they take turns talking about it, and that one of them has to find somebody who agrees with him or her before they get to talk about it.

Eventually, when people are together long enough, politics will become a way of carrying emotional material that people can’t name. It will be a fight about a schedule or committee or noise or food or some policy or other, but it won’t be about that.
e3-emuA:
This often comes about when the community realizes the importance of embracing a transformation from within. This gets funneled through a particular person, usually the founder, a teacher, a channel or some other special knower of how things really are.

The Farm , in Tennessee, at its largest about 1500 people, had many beautiful values. But, especially in the early days, the community’s spirituality and social life revolved around Stephen Gaskin. From what former members have shared, the “doctrine” ran very deep into the lives of community members. It’s one thing to talk about a universal consciousness. It’s another to not be able to escape the consciousness of one person’s opinions.
e3-emuB:
This occurs when a community decides that inner transformation is important, and that there needs to be a founder, teacher, channel or other special reality interpreter.

An example might be The Farm, a large (1,500 or so people) community in Tennessee. The Farm had many great aspects, but early on the spiritual and social life of the community revolved around Stephen Gaskin. According to former members, certain doctrines of the community were extremely pervasive in the decision making of members.
e4-emuA:
It’s a subtle reflection of two problems with existing groups: secular groups tend to be distributed and fail to be spiritual. Spiritual groups tend to be concentrated and succeed at being spiritual.

The actual problem in those latter two cases is that the authority people accrue in those roles bleeds over into the other roles. The founder of a community can’t also be the sole teacher. The teacher can’t also be the therapist. The farmer can’t also be the manager of the business. Etc.
e4-emuB:
It seems to be that both approaches fail for symmetric reasons. Secular approaches fail to address the inner life (while doing a good job at distributing power), whereas spiritual approaches do address the inner life but fail to distribute power.

Even more fundamentally, they fail to decouple these roles. If a person has earned power in one role (ie, a community leader/faith-healer, a therapist, a farmer, a business manager, etc), then they can translate that power to the other roles. In each case, it is concerning if a person has too much control over (a) identifying the problem, (b) controlling evidence related to the problem, (c) identifying a solution, and (d) making it costly to resist the solution or exit the situation.
e5-emuA:
What troubles me here is a general problem of authority bleed across modes. Someone is running a cult because they were a good teacher when they were running a school, or a good therapist when they were facilitating people dealing with difficult stuff in their life. Most of the economy runs because some people are good at farming, or at running a business. But it's a problem when someone has the ability to define the problem, control evidence about the problem, prescribe the solution to the problem, and make it hard for people to opt out or say no to the prescribed solution.

I want a way to work in depth that doesn't involve gurus, and a way of being in a community with distributed authority where people don't come in pre-healed, that also has peer practice and a playful aspect.
e5-emuB:
It seems like a related problem to me is cult leaders: someone has too much authority, or rather, has authority in multiple domains at once. The guru who is a good teacher, the therapist who really helps people, the farmer/business manager that actually has a lot of the economy in their hands. The problem happens when that person has the ability to define the problem, control all the information related to the problem, define what the solution is, and make it hard for people to leave or express disagreement.

I really like the idea of having depth while avoiding gurus, or distributed authority while not assuming people are fully emotionally developed, practicing with peers, and playing around.
